newsitem.title: INDIA: India stocks in small gains as lull in political crisis.
newsitem.headline: India stocks in small gains as lull in political crisis.

text.p: Indian stock markets on Thursday showed small gains following a lull in India's five-day old political crisis in which the government is facing a confidence vote in parliament, dealers said.
"The markets are moving sideways," said R. Ramakrishnan, chief dealer at ASK-Raymond James India Ltd. "There is not much downward pressure, but the market is stuck in a narrow band."

Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's 15-party minority coalition government must face a trust vote in parliament on April 11 after the Congress party on Sunday withdrew make-or-break support, plunging the country into political uncertainty.
In a day of dull trade due to a lack of political developments, pressure mounted on the Congress to strike a bargain with the government.

United Front and Congress leaders were holding secret meetings to explore a possible negotiated solution to the crisis, which has held hostage the path-breaking, tax-cutting budget for the 1997/98 fiscal year that started on April 1.
"Informal talks are on," United Front spokesman Jaipal Reddy told Reuters in New Delhi.
On Thursday, the Bombay Stock Exchange's benchmark 30-share index closed 19.19 points or 0.54 percent higher at a provisional 3.557.58.
The National Stock Exchange's 50-stock index was up 7.10 points or 0.71 percent at a provisional 1,009.30.

Shares of state-run Bharat Heavy Electrical Ltd (BHEL) surged 22.50 rupees, or seven percent, to 352.50 rupees after the firm on Thursday announced a 34 percent jump in its 1996/97 (April-March) net profit to 4.68 billion rupees.
The better-than expected annual results spurred hectic buying interest amid sharp volumes, traders said.

"The stock rocketed after the announcement of results. Speculators were aggressive bidders," said a dealer at a local brokerage. By close, more than 793,000 shares were traded at the Bombay Stock Exchange.
Brokers said they were pinning hopes on the safe passage of the 1997/98 (April-March) pro-business budget despite a current political crisis.
A broad consensus emerging among political parties to pass the budget through parliament helped firm the market mood, players said.
Parliament had earlier been scheduled to take up the budget on April 21.
